question: Wind farms are being built all across Europe, sometimes even against the wishes of local councillors and the general public. One example of this is the construction and operation of a wind energy project in Varrenes-Changy, which is taking place despite opposition from councillors, residents and the inquiry committee. This ideological shift towards green energy represents another step towards worldwide pollution.

This is a proven fact: many reports have revealed that these wind turbines are made with rare materials extracted from mines in non-EU countries (as is the case for cobalt). By importing these materials, the wind sector is contributing significantly to the destruction of ecosystems abroad, while also acting against the wishes of local councillors. In light of the above: 1.
Can the Commission detail the environmental impact of a wind turbine, from the extraction of its materials right up to its dismantling?
Is the Commission aware of cases where wind energy projects are being implemented despite objections from local councillors and the general public? If so, what does it intend to do?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (5.4.2024) Environmental impacts and circularity aspects of wind turbines are being extensively studied and are covered in reports produced by the European Commission’s Joint Research Centre1,2.

The sustainability assessment framework included in an Annex of the Clean Energy Technology Observatory (CETO) report covers such indicators as greenhouse gas emissions, water and land use, air quality and soil health.

Regarding waste management, Member States have to ensure that, like any other waste stream, the end of life of wind turbines is subject to waste management that complies with the Waste Framework Directive3, including the waste hierarchy set out in Article 4 of the Directive.

Without prejudice to the Commission’s role as guardian of the Treaties, Member States are primarily responsible for ensuring compliance with EU law, including in relation to public participation in decision-making.
